items.new: When I looked around the quarter-deck for someone in authority, so as to offer myself as a candidate for the voyage, at first I saw nobody. But I couldn't very well overlook a strange sort of tent, or rather wigwam, pitched a little behind the mainmast. It seemed to be only a temporary structure used in port. It was cone-shaped, some ten feet high, made of the long, huge slabs of flexible black bone taken from the middle and highest part of the right whale's jaws. A circle of these slabs, planted with their broad ends on the deck and laced together, sloped in toward one another and joined at the top in a tufted point, where the loose, hairy fibers waved back and forth like the topknot on the head of some old Pottowottamie Sachem, or chief. A triangular opening faced the bow of the ship, so that whoever sat inside had a complete view forward.

items.new: "Lost to a whale! Young man, come closer to me: it was devoured, chewed up, crunched by the most monstrous parmacetty that ever chipped a boat! — ah, ah!"

items.new: I was a little alarmed by his intensity, and perhaps also a little moved by the genuine grief in that final exclamation. But I said as calmly as I could, "What you say is no doubt true enough, sir. But how could I have known there was anything especially ferocious about that particular whale, though I might have guessed as much from the simple fact of the accident?"

items.new: But it was startling to see this kind-hearted Quaker woman come aboard on the last day carrying a long oil ladle in one hand and an even longer whaling lance in the other. Nor were Bildad and Captain Peleg any less busy. Bildad carried a long checklist of needed supplies, and at every delivery, he made a mark next to that item on his list. Every now and then, Peleg hobbled out of his whalebone den, roaring at the men down the hatchways, roaring up at the riggers on the masthead, and then concluded by roaring back into his wigwam.

items.reason: Misplaced modifier: as written, "in his broken way" attaches to Ishmael's questioning rather than to Queequeg's broken English. Moved the phrase to Queequeg's explanation.
items.new: Queequeg moved himself just past the sleeper's head and lit his tomahawk pipe. I sat at the feet. We passed the pipe back and forth over the sleeper between us. Meanwhile, when I questioned him, Queequeg explained in his broken way that in his land, due to the complete lack of benches and sofas, the king, chiefs, and important people had the custom of fattening some of the lower orders to serve as ottomans; and to furnish a house comfortably in that respect, you only had to buy up eight or ten lazy fellows and lay them around in the wall spaces between the windows and in the alcoves. Besides, they were very convenient on outings — much better than those garden chairs that fold into walking sticks. On occasion, a chief would simply call his attendant and order him to make himself into a bench under a spreading tree, perhaps in some damp marshy spot.

items.reason: "loath to depart, yet;" keeps the 1851 punctuation and word order and reads as a garble: the comma and semicolon split "depart yet" apart. Repunctuated to the edition's dash convention; content unchanged.
items.new: It was curious, and not unpleasing, how Peleg and Bildad were affected at this point, especially Captain Bildad. For he was loath to depart just yet — very loath to leave for good a ship bound on so long and perilous a voyage — beyond both stormy Capes; a ship in which some thousands of his hard-earned dollars were invested; a ship in which an old shipmate sailed as captain, a man almost as old as himself, setting out once more to meet all the terrors of the pitiless jaw; loath to say goodbye to a thing so brimful in every way of every interest to him — poor old Bildad lingered long. He paced the deck with anxious strides; ran down into the cabin to speak another farewell word there; came on deck again and looked to windward; looked toward the wide and endless waters, bounded only by the far-off, unseen Eastern Continents; looked toward the land; looked aloft; looked right and left; looked everywhere and nowhere; and at last, mechanically coiling a rope on its pin, he convulsively grasped stout Peleg by the hand and, holding up a lantern, stood for a moment gazing heroically into his face, as much as to say, "Nevertheless, friend Peleg, I can stand it; yes, I can."

items.reason: "a pleasant sun ... plenty of them" has a singular/plural mismatch, and "the tropic voyage you're going" is ungrammatical in modern English. Minimal grammatical repair.
items.new: "God bless you, and have you in His holy keeping, men," murmured old Bildad, almost incoherently. "I hope you'll have fine weather now, so that Captain Ahab may soon be moving among you — a pleasant sun is all he needs, and you'll have plenty of that on the tropic voyage you're making. Be careful in the hunt, you mates. Don't stave the boats needlessly, you harpooners; good white cedar plank has gone up a full three percent within the year. Don't forget your prayers, either. Mr. Starbuck, mind that cooper doesn't waste the spare staves. Oh! The sail needles are in the green locker! Don't whale it too much on the Lord's days, men; but don't miss a fair chance either — that's rejecting Heaven's good gifts. Keep an eye on the molasses cask, Mr. Stubb; it was a little leaky, I thought. If you touch at the islands, Mr. Flask, beware of fornication. Goodbye, goodbye! Don't keep that cheese too long down in the hold, Mr. Starbuck; it'll spoil. Be careful with the butter — twenty cents a pound it was, and mind you, if —"
